cards.title: Gyeong-In Yu
cards.body: Gyeong-In Yu and Joo Seong Jeong of Seoul National University, Soojeong Kim of FriendliAI, and Geon-Woo Kim and Byung-Gon Chun of both. They were not proposing a faster kernel. Their claim was that the interface between a serving system and its execution engine — hand over a batch, get a batch back — was the wrong shape for autoregressive generation.
cards.prompt: Orca introduced two named techniques, not one. Name both, and say which of them exists only because the other one does.
cards.answer: Iteration-level scheduling — run the engine for a single decoding iteration and re-pick the batch — and selective batching, which applies batching only to a selected set of operations. Selective batching exists to make iteration-level scheduling possible: once the sequences in a batch are at different lengths, not every operation can be batched over them.

cards.title: The convoy, priced
cards.body: The end-to-end run: GPT-3 175B across 16 NVIDIA 40-GB A100s, two Azure ND96asr A100 v4 VMs. Held to a median normalized latency of 190 ms, FasterTransformer delivered 0.185 req/s and Orca delivered 6.81 — a 36.9× speedup. Nothing about the hardware or the weights changed. Only who was allowed in the batch, and when.
cards.prompt: At matched median latency on GPT-3 175B, on the same 16 GPUs, give the throughput NVIDIA FasterTransformer reached and the throughput Orca reached, in requests per second — and the ratio between them.
cards.answer: 0.185 req/s for FasterTransformer against 6.81 req/s for Orca, at a median latency of 190 ms per generated token: a 36.9× speedup. Same 16 40-GB A100s, same model, purely a scheduling change.

cards.title: Orca, OSDI '22
cards.body: Yu, Jeong, Kim, Kim and Chun, "Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models", 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation, July 11-13 2022, Carlsbad, California. Open access from USENIX. Algorithm 1 is the scheduler; the reservation the story ends on is lines 23-26 of it.
cards.prompt: Name the paper that introduced iteration-level scheduling — exact title, conference, year. Then say what its scheduler reserved at admission time, and on what basis it sized the reservation.
cards.answer: "Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models", 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI '22), 2022. Its scheduler reserved max_tokens slots of GPU memory for keys and values in advance — sized to the maximum tokens the request could ever have, not to what it actually generated.

cards.title: The paper that shipped without code
cards.body: Orca shipped as a paper, not as code. Building vLLM in 2023, Kwon et al. had to rebuild it to have anything to benchmark against. Their verdict: interleaving requests "makes memory management more challenging, making the techniques proposed in vLLM even more crucial." Everyone calls it continuous batching now; the Orca paper never uses that phrase.
cards.prompt: Orca's implementation was never released. What did that force the vLLM team to build in 2023, and what did they conclude about the effect of Orca-style fine-grained scheduling on memory management?
cards.answer: They wrote their own Orca purely as a baseline — "Since Orca is not publicly available for use, we implement our own version of Orca" — and concluded that fine-grained interleaving makes memory management harder, not easier. That is the gap PagedAttention was built to close, which is why the scheduler story and the allocator story are one story.
